items.english: To note it in passing, Liu was not at all a man who delighted in visitors. But when he already had one visitor with him, and a new visitor came, he would generally receive him gladly. He had a childish vanity of the sort that might be described as showing off the fact of having a visitor before a visitor. Besides, today's barbarian monk was at this time the talk everywhere. He was by no means a visitor one would be ashamed to meet. — Liu's motives in saying he would meet him lay roughly here.

notes: The text gives no speaker for p15-p16; left unattributed as in the source. Read as talk between Liu and Sun Sensei.

items.english: "Alms-seeking, most likely. He will be asking for some charity, I suppose."
notes: The text gives no speaker for p15-p16; left unattributed as in the source.

items.english: While the two were talking such things over between them, presently there entered, guided in by the yahuan, a monk of strange aspect, tall and with eyes like cut violet quartz. He wore a yellow robe, his grown-out curling hair hanging tiresomely over his shoulders. Still holding his red-handled shubi, he planted himself heavily in the middle of the room. He offered no greeting, nor did he speak.
notes: Kept yahuan for the young maidservant and shubi for the fly-whisk, as standing terms; sense is given by context.

items.english: Liu hesitated for a while, but as that somehow grew unsettling to him, he ventured, "Have you some business with me?"
Whereupon the barbarian monk said, "You are the one, I take it, who is fond of wine."

"I am." The question was so abrupt that Liu, as he gave his vague answer, looked toward Sun Sensei as if seeking rescue. Sun Sensei, with a composed air, went on laying stones on the board by himself. He showed no disposition to take any part.
"You are afflicted with a rare disease. Are you aware of it?" the barbarian monk said, as if to make sure. Liu, hearing of a disease, made a dubious face, and, stroking his bamboo wife,
notes: Bamboo wife is a hollow bamboo bolster embraced in summer; the sentence runs on into p22.
